text: Linear models in the last lesson assume the relationship between features and returns is additive. Real financial relationships are often not. Momentum might only predict well when volatility is low, or a value factor might only work in certain rate regimes. Decision trees and random forests can capture exactly these kinds of conditional, non-linear interactions without you having to hand specify them.

A decision tree repeatedly splits the data on feature thresholds to minimize prediction error at each step. Left unconstrained, it can grow until each leaf contains just one or two examples, fitting the training data almost perfectly, including its noise. In a domain where real signal explains only one to two percent of variance, an unconstrained tree will happily memorize the other ninety eight percent that's pure noise. Max depth and minimum samples per leaf are the controls that keep that from happening.

A random forest fits many trees, each on a bootstrap resampled subset of rows and a random subset of features at each split, then averages their predictions. Because each tree overfits to different noise, averaging many of them cancels out a lot of that noise while the real, shared signal, if there is any, survives the averaging. It's a textbook variance reduction technique.

Even with that built in variance reduction, constraining depth and leaf size still matters on noisy financial data, the averaging helps but doesn't make unlimited depth safe. Random forests also expose feature importances, a quick measure of how much each feature contributed to reducing error. It's a useful first pass, but it has real limitations, and chapter five covers more robust alternatives like permutation importance and shap values in depth.

Trees and forests capture relationships linear models miss, and averaging many de-correlated trees tames the overfitting a single tree invites. Up next, lesson seven: gradient boosting on financial features, where trees get combined sequentially instead of averaged.
